trades-etf-1.title: P1 · 01 · Build a Stand for an Instruction Card
trades-etf-1.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

Make one triangular stand for a 3 × 5-in card, then improve its card-supporting lip. The 5-in card edge rests horizontally on the 4-in-wide stand.

Why: A technician must turn a flat pattern into a useful object. Today you will read a cut/fold plan, measure fractions from one datum and check whether the product works.

  1. One labeled triangular stand with a 3 × 5-in card; the spare lip beside it.
  2. Notebook: labeled side view, actual F/B lengths, and a two-row table: lip depth | trial 1 | trial 2 | trial 3. Save the individual transfer answer in the app.

110 minutes / two periods. Seven crews for 15 students: six pairs and one trio. Rotate marker, maker and checker; each student keeps their own graph notebook and completes one digital transfer answer.

Daily kit and preparation

Per crew: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Two folder-card rectangles at least 10 1/2 × 4 in, one 4 × 1-in lip blank, one 4 × 1 1/2-in replacement lip blank, one paper/card rectangle 3 × 5 in, and 24 in of tape. Keep unused stock for a remake.

Class quantities: prepare seven of these kits; each student has their own tape, pencil and notebook. Shared stations are identified explicitly above.

Set out seven kits, 15 notebooks and seven printed A sheets. Prebuild one finished sample and one unfolded labeled blank. Use 10 1/2-in stock, not a 10-in strip. A normal opened folder supplies the length.

Project equipment and continuity

For 15 students use six pairs and one trio: seven crew trays. Every student measures and draws; rotate marker, cutter and checker. The trio rotates all three roles. Rehearse the specified build before teaching; the directions are authored construction plans, not a claim of physical validation.

Show this before students start

Say: “We are making THIS card stand. The 4-in panel goes on the table.” Show the completed sample before the flat plan. Model one mark from datum A, form the triangular loop, then show where T overlaps F and where L attaches. Release cutting only after both long edges have matching fold marks.

Open labeled assembly / test drawing

Learning targets

  1. I can calculate fractional dimensions, clearance, material area and cost for a useful product.
  2. I can measure, lay out and inspect organizer parts from a consistent reference.
  3. I can interpret and revise dimensioned part drawings, views and cut lists.
  4. I can build, user-test and physically improve a useful organizer.

0–10 min · Brief · Today’s exact job

  1. Why this job: A technician must turn a flat pattern into a useful object. Today you will read a cut/fold plan, measure fractions from one datum and check whether the product works.
  2. Required today: Make one triangular stand for a 3 × 5-in card, then improve its card-supporting lip. The 5-in card edge rests horizontally on the 4-in-wide stand.
  3. Look at the supplied labeled drawing. Find the finished object or test setup before starting.
  4. Read the kit list. Take the listed continuing project out of storage; name missing items before beginning.

Notebook: Title/date; one sentence naming today’s exact object and its purpose.

10–25 min · Measure · Measure and mark

  1. Cut the test card to 3 × 5 in. Mark its 5-in edge BOTTOM. The load today is this card.
  2. On the body stock, choose the left 4-in edge as datum A. Mark 0, 3, 6, 10 and 10 1/2 in along BOTH long edges, always measuring from A.
  3. Join matching marks with straight lines. Check overall width 4 in and length 10 1/2 in with your partner; then swap who reads the tape.

Notebook: Feature | required value | actual value | units | datum/endpoints. Keep repeat readings.

25–40 min · Plan · Read the plan and work the math

  1. Label F between 0–3 in, R between 3–6, B between 6–10, and T between 10–10 1/2. Do not cut the three inside lines.
  2. Sketch the finished triangular side view in your notebook: two 3-in sloping faces and a 4-in base. Add the 1/2-in overlap tab on a separate detail.

Notebook: Use the named sketch/table in the directions. Label views, dimensions, units and revision.

40–85 min · Make · Numbered bench directions

  1. Cut the OUTSIDE of the 10 1/2 × 4-in blank. Write your crew name on B.
  2. Fold at 3, 6 and 10 in, all toward the same side of the card. Press the creases against a ruler; do not cut or score with a blade.
  3. Place B flat on the desk. Bring the free edge of F to the fold between B and T. The 3-in faces meet at the top; the cross-section is a triangle.
  4. Put T inside F, overlapping it by 1/2 in. Tape the seam across the full 4-in width. The tab is a joint, not a fourth side.
  5. Cut L to 4 × 1 in. Draw and fold a line along its length, making two 4 × 1/2-in halves.
  6. Tape one half of L to F at the bottom of the front face, with the lip fold at the front/base corner. Leave the other half projecting forward as a shelf; adjust that shelf approximately level with the tabletop.
  7. Rest the card’s BOTTOM edge on L and lean the card back against F. Center it: about 1/2 in of card extends beyond each side of the stand.
  8. Run the first three-trial test. Then cut a second lip 4 × 1 1/2 in; fold 1/2 in from one long edge. Replace L, attaching the 1/2-in half to F so the shelf is now 1 in deep. Label the new lip revision B.
  9. Repeat the identical test. Keep the better lip on the stand; retain the removed lip with your notebook. If the body failed, remake it to the original dimensions before comparing lips.

Notebook: Label made parts and note any changed dimension. A short labeled sketch is enough; do not write an essay.

85–100 min · Test · Test and inspect

  1. Trial: put the stand on a level desk, place the card, remove both hands and time 10 seconds. Pass only if both stand and card stay upright. Remove the card; repeat for three trials.
  2. Do three trials for the 1/2-in lip, then three for the 1-in lip. Record each pass/fail; a tie is a valid result.
  3. Measure F and B along their fold-to-fold edges. Classroom layout check: 3 in and 4 in, each within ±1/8 in. Correct a wrong fold even if the card happens to stand.

Notebook: Copy the specified trial table; include each pass/fail or measured value and the change made.

100–110 min · Explain · Show the finished work

  1. Put these on the bench: One labeled triangular stand with a 3 × 5-in card; the spare lip beside it.
  2. Notebook: labeled side view, actual F/B lengths, and a two-row table: lip depth | trial 1 | trial 2 | trial 3. Save the individual transfer answer in the app.
  3. Complete the independent transfer problem below. These supplied numbers are practice values; they do not change the required build dimensions.
  4. A revised stand uses two 3 1/4-in faces, a 4-in base and a 1/2-in joining tab. Find its blank length. Explain where you would measure the second fold from datum A. Cite your notebook and one test result.
  5. Save one short individual answer with units, working and notebook page/date. Show the teacher your own physical measurement and plan interpretation. Store the labeled project and return shared supplies.

Notebook: Individual transfer calculation with units + page/date containing the practical evidence.

Teacher inspection points

At minute 25 inspect 3/6/10-in marks. At minute 40 each student points to F/R/B/T on the blank. By minute 70 expect a standing triangle; by 95 expect six recorded trials. Ask each student to show the zero reference and read one fraction without a partner.

If the build does not work

Four-sided loop → T was treated as a panel; overlap it inside F. Card slides → shelf must project below the card, not be taped flat against F. Stand rocks → straighten the seam and check B is the 4-in panel. No apparent improvement → record the tie; do not invent a failure.

Worked trades math · supplied practice values

  1. How much of the strip makes the three sides?
  2. 10 1/2 − 1/2 = 10 in; 3 + 3 + 4 = 10 in.
  3. The joining tab overlaps; it is not a fourth side of the triangular stand.

Teacher answer key and interpretation

Blank = 3 1/4 + 3 1/4 + 4 + 1/2 = 11 in. Second fold is 6 1/2 in from datum A. Actual tests vary; inspect independent tape use and a real revision, not only the digital answer.

Individual practical evidence

  1. Math: inspect the individual operation, units and reasonableness check.
  2. Measuring: observe the student place/read the tool using the specified datum and endpoints.
  3. Plan reading: ask the student to find one labeled dimension or connection on both drawing and object.
  4. Build/revision: inspect the actual part, recorded test and named repair. Record independent / with cue / not observed separately; a crew result is not an individual demonstration.

Scope and support

Complete the specified baseline and test first. Only the revision described in this lesson is required. Use a large drawing, fraction strip or oral rehearsal as support, then collect a fresh independent check. Do not fill missing apparatus, dimensions or readings with guesses. Teacher equipment rehearsal checks local stock and kit fit before release; these authored designs have not been physically piloted by the curriculum author.

trades-etf-1.title: P1 · 02 · Mock Up a Three-Bay Supply Tray
trades-etf-1.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

Build a folder-card tray with three side-by-side bays for erasers, binder clips and paper clips. Keep this version for comparison.

Why: Storage fit depends on inside clearance, not just outside size. This prototype gives us a real fit problem to measure before using stronger material.

  1. One three-bay folder tray with seven labeled parts and the supplies in it.
  2. Notebook: top view, six clearance readings, retrieval results and one circled problem.

110 minutes / two periods. Seven crews for 15 students: six pairs and one trio. Rotate marker, maker and checker; each student keeps their own graph notebook and completes one digital transfer answer.

Daily kit and preparation

Per crew: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Folder card for the seven parts in drawing B; two erasers, three binder clips and six paper clips; 36 in of tape. B = base 8 × 6 in; F and R = two long walls 8 × 2 in; E1, E2, D1 and D2 = four short-wall blanks 6 × 2 in. Trim short walls to the measured gap between F and R.

Class quantities: prepare seven of these kits; each student has their own tape, pencil and notebook. Shared stations are identified explicitly above.

Provide ordinary folder stock and identical test supplies in all seven kits. Cut a sample short wall to show fitting between F/R. Do not substitute a free-choice organizer brief.

Project equipment and continuity

For 15 students use six pairs and one trio: seven crew trays. Every student measures and draws; rotate marker, cutter and checker. The trio rotates all three roles. Rehearse the specified build before teaching; the directions are authored construction plans, not a claim of physical validation.

Show this before students start

Show why a 6-in short-wall blank must be trimmed when long walls occupy part of the 6-in base. Demonstrate dry fitting, marking and trimming one end. Point to “outside” and “clear” on the real tray.

Open labeled assembly / test drawing

Learning targets

  1. I can calculate fractional dimensions, clearance, material area and cost for a useful product.
  2. I can measure, lay out and inspect organizer parts from a consistent reference.
  3. I can interpret and revise dimensioned part drawings, views and cut lists.
  4. I can build, user-test and physically improve a useful organizer.

0–10 min · Brief · Today’s exact job

  1. Why this job: Storage fit depends on inside clearance, not just outside size. This prototype gives us a real fit problem to measure before using stronger material.
  2. Required today: Build a folder-card tray with three side-by-side bays for erasers, binder clips and paper clips. Keep this version for comparison.
  3. Look at the supplied labeled drawing. Find the finished object or test setup before starting.
  4. Read the kit list. Take the listed continuing project out of storage; name missing items before beginning.

Notebook: Title/date; one sentence naming today’s exact object and its purpose.

10–25 min · Measure · Measure and mark

  1. Measure the three types of supplies at their widest point. Make a table: item | width | unit.
  2. Mark the base 8 × 6 in. From its left edge, mark lines at 2 5/8 and 5 1/4 in across the base; these locate the LEFT faces of D1 and D2.

Notebook: Feature | required value | actual value | units | datum/endpoints. Keep repeat readings.

25–40 min · Plan · Read the plan and work the math

  1. Draw an 8 × 6-in top view. Label the front edge F and the left outer edge datum A.
  2. Copy the seven-part list. Assign left bay = erasers, middle = binder clips, right = paper clips. This is the required first arrangement.

Notebook: Use the named sketch/table in the directions. Label views, dimensions, units and revision.

40–85 min · Make · Numbered bench directions

  1. Cut B, F and R to their labeled sizes. Cut E1/E2/D1/D2 initially as 6 × 2-in rectangles.
  2. Stand F and R on TOP of B, with their outside faces flush to its front and rear edges. Tape each wall to B inside and outside; keep walls upright.
  3. Set E1 between F and R at the left edge. Mark the actual inside gap on E1; trim to that mark so it fits without bending F/R. Use it to mark the other three short walls, then check each fit.
  4. Tape E1/E2 upright with outside faces flush to the left/right edges of B.
  5. Tape D1/D2 upright with their LEFT faces on the two base lines. Tape both ends to F/R and bottom edges to B.
  6. Put the assigned supplies in their bays. Partner removes and returns each type three times while the tray stays on the desk.
  7. Circle one snag on your notebook top view. Write one specific proposed repair: loose joint → reinforce; object catches divider → move that divider 1/4 in. Keep the prototype intact for day 3.

Notebook: Label made parts and note any changed dimension. A short labeled sketch is enough; do not write an essay.

85–100 min · Test · Test and inspect

  1. Each type fits its assigned bay and can be removed without lifting the tray. Record three attempts for each type.
  2. Measure each clear bay between wall faces at the front and rear. Record the six readings, even if they are unequal.

Notebook: Copy the specified trial table; include each pass/fail or measured value and the change made.

100–110 min · Explain · Show the finished work

  1. Put these on the bench: One three-bay folder tray with seven labeled parts and the supplies in it.
  2. Notebook: top view, six clearance readings, retrieval results and one circled problem.
  3. Complete the independent transfer problem below. These supplied numbers are practice values; they do not change the required build dimensions.
  4. Two clear bays each need 3 1/4 in. One internal partition is 1/8 in and two outer walls are each 1/8 in. Calculate outside width and identify the internal partition on your sketch.
  5. Save one short individual answer with units, working and notebook page/date. Show the teacher your own physical measurement and plan interpretation. Store the labeled project and return shared supplies.

Notebook: Individual transfer calculation with units + page/date containing the practical evidence.

Teacher inspection points

Check F/R sit on the base, partitions run front-to-back, and all students can identify the same datum. Accept small unequal bays for thin stock; the 2 1/2-in example assumes 1/8-in stock.

If the build does not work

Walls bow → the short pieces are too long; dry-fit and trim. Bay narrows toward rear → divider is angled; retape square to F. Supplies snag → mark the actual contact, not a vague “bad fit.”

Worked trades math · supplied practice values

  1. Find the interior and outside width of three clear bays.
  2. 3 × 2 1/2 + 2 × 1/8 = 7 3/4 in interior; + 2 × 1/8 = 8 in outside.
  3. Only the two internal partitions belong in the interior-width sum.

Teacher answer key and interpretation

Outside width = 6 1/2 + 3/8 = 6 7/8 in. Interior width = 6 5/8 in. Check that the student adds three thicknesses for the outside width, not two.

Individual practical evidence

  1. Math: inspect the individual operation, units and reasonableness check.
  2. Measuring: observe the student place/read the tool using the specified datum and endpoints.
  3. Plan reading: ask the student to find one labeled dimension or connection on both drawing and object.
  4. Build/revision: inspect the actual part, recorded test and named repair. Record independent / with cue / not observed separately; a crew result is not an individual demonstration.

Scope and support

Complete the specified baseline and test first. Only the revision described in this lesson is required. Use a large drawing, fraction strip or oral rehearsal as support, then collect a fresh independent check. Do not fill missing apparatus, dimensions or readings with guesses. Teacher equipment rehearsal checks local stock and kit fit before release; these authored designs have not been physically piloted by the curriculum author.

trades-etf-1.title: P1 · 03 · Measure and Cut the Durable Tray Parts
trades-etf-1.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

Make the seven fitted parts for a stronger copy of the same three-bay tray; dry-fit them before assembly.

Why: Fabricators use a cut list to avoid wasting stock. You will transfer dimensions and account for the actual wall thickness.

  1. Seven labeled durable parts that dry-fit the tray plan.
  2. Notebook: stock layout, complete final cut list and two inspection readings per student.

110 minutes / two periods. Seven crews for 15 students: six pairs and one trio. Rotate marker, maker and checker; each student keeps their own graph notebook and completes one digital transfer answer.

Daily kit and preparation

Per crew: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Previous prototype, clean thin packaging card totaling at least 130 in² of usable area per crew, and 12 in of temporary tape. B = base 8 × 6 in; F and R = two long walls 8 × 2 in; E1, E2, D1 and D2 = four short-wall blanks 6 × 2 in. Trim short walls to the measured gap between F and R.

Class quantities: prepare seven of these kits; each student has their own tape, pencil and notebook. Shared stations are identified explicitly above.

Collect seven sets of thin, clean packaging card that scissors can cut. Adult-precut thick corrugated material; do not introduce utility knives to this lesson. Supply two spare short-wall blanks per crew.

Project equipment and continuity

For 15 students use six pairs and one trio: seven crew trays. Every student measures and draws; rotate marker, cutter and checker. The trio rotates all three roles. Rehearse the specified build before teaching; the directions are authored construction plans, not a claim of physical validation.

Show this before students start

Model measuring the actual inside gap with a story strip. Compare the physical gap with the example 6 − 2(1/8) = 5 3/4 in. Explain that their fitted length comes from their own stock.

Open labeled assembly / test drawing

Learning targets

  1. I can calculate fractional dimensions, clearance, material area and cost for a useful product.
  2. I can measure, lay out and inspect organizer parts from a consistent reference.
  3. I can interpret and revise dimensioned part drawings, views and cut lists.
  4. I can build, user-test and physically improve a useful organizer.

0–10 min · Brief · Today’s exact job

  1. Why this job: Fabricators use a cut list to avoid wasting stock. You will transfer dimensions and account for the actual wall thickness.
  2. Required today: Make the seven fitted parts for a stronger copy of the same three-bay tray; dry-fit them before assembly.
  3. Look at the supplied labeled drawing. Find the finished object or test setup before starting.
  4. Read the kit list. Take the listed continuing project out of storage; name missing items before beginning.

Notebook: Title/date; one sentence naming today’s exact object and its purpose.

10–25 min · Measure · Measure and mark

  1. Measure usable stock. Lay out 8 × 6 base, two 8 × 2 walls and four 6 × 2 blanks; each student marks at least one part.
  2. Mark D1/D2 positions at 2 5/8 and 5 1/4 in from the base’s left edge. Check both endpoints before drawing each line.

Notebook: Feature | required value | actual value | units | datum/endpoints. Keep repeat readings.

25–40 min · Plan · Read the plan and work the math

  1. Make a cut-list table: part | quantity | blank length | height/depth | final fitted length. Enter B×1, F/R×2, E/D×4.
  2. Draw the rectangles on available stock with no overlaps. Shared scissors cuts need no added saw kerf. Preserve long straight offcuts.

Notebook: Use the named sketch/table in the directions. Label views, dimensions, units and revision.

40–85 min · Make · Numbered bench directions

  1. Cut B, F and R first. Label each part on the face that will be outside.
  2. Temporarily tape F/R upright on B with outer faces flush to the base edges.
  3. Use a narrow scrap strip to capture the inside gap: hold one end against F, mark where it meets the inside face of R, then measure that length.
  4. Transfer that gap to all four short-wall blanks. Mark a waste X on the portion to remove.
  5. Partner checks the first marked short wall; trim it and test it between F/R without bending either wall.
  6. Trim the remaining three to the same checked length. Label E1/E2/D1/D2.
  7. Dry-fit all seven pieces in their specified positions. Do not permanently tape partitions today. Bundle small parts in the base with the cut list.

Notebook: Label made parts and note any changed dimension. A short labeled sketch is enough; do not write an essay.

85–100 min · Test · Test and inspect

  1. Each short wall fits between F/R without force and with no end gap greater than 1/8 in.
  2. Check one 8-in part and one fitted part independently. Record intended, actual and signed difference; ±1/8 in is the classroom cutting tolerance.

Notebook: Copy the specified trial table; include each pass/fail or measured value and the change made.

100–110 min · Explain · Show the finished work

  1. Put these on the bench: Seven labeled durable parts that dry-fit the tray plan.
  2. Notebook: stock layout, complete final cut list and two inspection readings per student.
  3. Complete the independent transfer problem below. These supplied numbers are practice values; they do not change the required build dimensions.
  4. A 12 × 9-in sheet supplies six 4 × 3-in pieces. Show an arrangement, calculate used area and remaining area, and explain why the layout matters.
  5. Save one short individual answer with units, working and notebook page/date. Show the teacher your own physical measurement and plan interpretation. Store the labeled project and return shared supplies.

Notebook: Individual transfer calculation with units + page/date containing the practical evidence.

Teacher inspection points

Inspect one cut per student before the rest are cut. The list must name which parts share the same fitted length; students may not silently use 6 in for all four.

If the build does not work

Too short → replace that part using a spare; tape cannot restore a missing wall length accurately. Too long → mark and trim only the excess. Stock too thick for scissors → teacher substitutes thinner card or supplies precut blanks.

Worked trades math · supplied practice values

  1. Can four rectangular pieces fit this sheet?
  2. Each 4 × 3-in piece has 12 in² area; four use 48 in². Two rows of two fit in an 8 × 6-in rectangle.
  3. A 9 × 12-in sheet can contain this arrangement. Area alone would not prove a different set of shapes fits.

Teacher answer key and interpretation

Three columns of 4 in and two rows of 3 in fit: 12 × 6 in. Used area 72 in²; sheet 108 in²; remaining 36 in². An equivalent rotated layout is acceptable.

Individual practical evidence

  1. Math: inspect the individual operation, units and reasonableness check.
  2. Measuring: observe the student place/read the tool using the specified datum and endpoints.
  3. Plan reading: ask the student to find one labeled dimension or connection on both drawing and object.
  4. Build/revision: inspect the actual part, recorded test and named repair. Record independent / with cue / not observed separately; a crew result is not an individual demonstration.

Scope and support

Complete the specified baseline and test first. Only the revision described in this lesson is required. Use a large drawing, fraction strip or oral rehearsal as support, then collect a fresh independent check. Do not fill missing apparatus, dimensions or readings with guesses. Teacher equipment rehearsal checks local stock and kit fit before release; these authored designs have not been physically piloted by the curriculum author.

trades-etf-1.title: P1 · 04 · Assemble and Reinforce the Supply Tray
trades-etf-1.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

Assemble the durable tray and add four folded corner reinforcements; compare it with the folder prototype.

Why: A stronger joint consumes material and time. You will make that change deliberately and calculate a transparent classroom material cost.

  1. An assembled durable three-bay tray with four angle brackets; prototype retained.
  2. Notebook: before/after retrieval table, finished dimensions and actual tape-use calculation.

110 minutes / two periods. Seven crews for 15 students: six pairs and one trio. Rotate marker, maker and checker; each student keeps their own graph notebook and completes one digital transfer answer.

Daily kit and preparation

Per crew: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Seven durable parts from day 3, prototype, four 2 × 2-in card squares, the same test supplies, and a measured 48-in tape allowance.

Class quantities: prepare seven of these kits; each student has their own tape, pencil and notebook. Shared stations are identified explicitly above.

Have seven 48-in tape strips on backing sheets plus replacement stock for failed joints. State that the tape allowance is a measurement budget, not a reason to leave a needed repair unsafe or incomplete.

Project equipment and continuity

For 15 students use six pairs and one trio: seven crew trays. Every student measures and draws; rotate marker, cutter and checker. The trio rotates all three roles. Rehearse the specified build before teaching; the directions are authored construction plans, not a claim of physical validation.

Show this before students start

Show a flat square becoming an inside-corner bracket. Demonstrate that the two legs join two different walls. Calculate one sample area and convert 24 in of tape to 2 ft.

Open labeled assembly / test drawing

Learning targets

  1. I can calculate fractional dimensions, clearance, material area and cost for a useful product.
  2. I can measure, lay out and inspect organizer parts from a consistent reference.
  3. I can interpret and revise dimensioned part drawings, views and cut lists.
  4. I can build, user-test and physically improve a useful organizer.

0–10 min · Brief · Today’s exact job

  1. Why this job: A stronger joint consumes material and time. You will make that change deliberately and calculate a transparent classroom material cost.
  2. Required today: Assemble the durable tray and add four folded corner reinforcements; compare it with the folder prototype.
  3. Look at the supplied labeled drawing. Find the finished object or test setup before starting.
  4. Read the kit list. Take the listed continuing project out of storage; name missing items before beginning.

Notebook: Title/date; one sentence naming today’s exact object and its purpose.

10–25 min · Measure · Measure and mark

  1. Measure and mark the four 2 × 2-in squares and their 1-in center folds.
  2. Record starting tape allowance 48 in; measure unused tape at the end. Use the final cut-list dimensions, not the raw blank sizes, for area.

Notebook: Feature | required value | actual value | units | datum/endpoints. Keep repeat readings.

25–40 min · Plan · Read the plan and work the math

  1. Copy revision B onto the top view and mark the four reinforced outside corners.
  2. Set up a material table: card area (in²), tape used (in), tape used ÷ 12 (ft). The worked example uses supplied classroom prices, not actual store prices.

Notebook: Use the named sketch/table in the directions. Label views, dimensions, units and revision.

40–85 min · Make · Numbered bench directions

  1. Tape F/R to B, then fit and tape E1/E2 using the checked part lengths.
  2. Put D1/D2 left faces on their marked lines; tape bottoms and ends.
  3. Fold each reinforcing square 90 degrees along its centerline.
  4. Fit one bracket vertically inside each outer corner. Tape one leg to the long wall and one to the end wall; leave the bottom against B.
  5. Move the same supplies from the prototype into the same labeled bays.
  6. Run the retrieval test on both versions. If a reinforced corner catches an object, trim only the projecting tape and retest.
  7. Measure remaining tape and calculate used length. Label the durable tray revision B and retain prototype A.

Notebook: Label made parts and note any changed dimension. A short labeled sketch is enough; do not write an essay.

85–100 min · Test · Test and inspect

  1. For each version, remove/return each supply type three times. Count snags and loose joints using the same operator and objects.
  2. Measure outside width and one clear bay. Check that reinforcement did not block the assigned objects.

Notebook: Copy the specified trial table; include each pass/fail or measured value and the change made.

100–110 min · Explain · Show the finished work

  1. Put these on the bench: An assembled durable three-bay tray with four angle brackets; prototype retained.
  2. Notebook: before/after retrieval table, finished dimensions and actual tape-use calculation.
  3. Complete the independent transfer problem below. These supplied numbers are practice values; they do not change the required build dimensions.
  4. Your build consumes 3/4 sheet at a classroom price of $2.40 per sheet and 4 ft of tape at $0.10/ft. Find consumed-material cost and the purchase cost if you must buy one sheet plus that tape.
  5. Save one short individual answer with units, working and notebook page/date. Show the teacher your own physical measurement and plan interpretation. Store the labeled project and return shared supplies.

Notebook: Individual transfer calculation with units + page/date containing the practical evidence.

Teacher inspection points

Look for real corner brackets, unchanged test objects, and a measured tape remainder. Both students must name a changed joint and explain the purpose.

If the build does not work

Bracket blocks a bay → flatten it tightly against the corner; remove protruding tape. Tray still flexes → check the wall-to-base seam before adding decorative layers. Cost differs from example → use their measured quantity and the explicitly supplied price.

Worked trades math · supplied practice values

  1. Estimate the cost using classroom prices, not a supplier quote.
  2. 0.50 sheet × $2.40/sheet + 3 ft × $0.10/ft = $1.50.
  3. This is material consumed. Buying one whole sheet would cost $2.40 before tape or other supplies.

Teacher answer key and interpretation

Consumed cost = $1.80 + $0.40 = $2.20. Whole-sheet purchase = $2.40 + $0.40 = $2.80. Do not present sample prices as current quotations.

Individual practical evidence

trades-etf-2.title: P2 · 01 · Build and Load-Test Two Paper Towers
trades-etf-2.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

Build two 11-in paper columns supporting a 6 × 6-in platform; add base ties and repeat the same capped load test.

Why: Builders need a continuous load path and stable supports. A capped test shows what the model carried under specified conditions.

  1. One tower with two triangular columns and removable base ties.
  2. Two load records and an annotated load-path sketch.

110 minutes / two periods. Seven crews for 15 students: six pairs and one trio. Rotate marker, maker and checker; each student keeps their own graph notebook and completes one digital transfer answer.

Daily kit and preparation

Per crew: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Two letter sheets for two 6 1/2 × 11-in column blanks, two 6 × 1-in offcut ties, one 6 × 6-in card platform, one small paper cup, ten identical large paper clips and 36 in of tape.

Class quantities: prepare seven of these kits; each student has their own tape, pencil and notebook. Shared stations are identified explicitly above.

Prebuild one sample using the actual paper. Use large paper clips as identical low-mass loads; count rather than infer newtons. Test at tabletop height with the area clear of faces.

Project equipment and continuity

Use seven crew trays. Reserve a permitted classroom survey area. Collect the daily kits before release. Keep the supplied model dimensions separate from actual school measurements. These are classroom models, not full-size construction designs.

Show this before students start

Show the 1/2-in column overlap and level ends. Trace load from cup to platform, columns and tabletop. Explain when to stop and how to record a capped result.

Open labeled assembly / test drawing

Learning targets

  1. I can convert feet/inches, scale dimensions, and calculate building quantities and performance change.
  2. I can survey a space and check model dimensions, openings and structural/thermal tests.
  3. I can interpret coordinated floor plans, elevations, details, symbols and scale.
  4. I can build and improve a model building using structural and thermal test evidence.

0–10 min · Brief · Today’s exact job

  1. Why this job: Builders need a continuous load path and stable supports. A capped test shows what the model carried under specified conditions.
  2. Required today: Build two 11-in paper columns supporting a 6 × 6-in platform; add base ties and repeat the same capped load test.
  3. Look at the supplied labeled drawing. Find the finished object or test setup before starting.
  4. Read the kit list. Take the listed continuing project out of storage; name missing items before beginning.

Notebook: Title/date; one sentence naming today’s exact object and its purpose.

10–25 min · Measure · Measure and mark

  1. Mark both blanks from the same long edge at 2/4/6 in; measure height 11 in.
  2. Draw a 6 × 6-in footprint on scrap. Keep both columns and platform inside it.

Notebook: Feature | required value | actual value | units | datum/endpoints. Keep repeat readings.

25–40 min · Plan · Read the plan and work the math

  1. Sketch the side and top views; show the two triangular column footprints under the left/right sides of the platform.
  2. Prepare a load table with rows 0 through 10 clips for version A and B. The cup/platform are the same in both tests.

Notebook: Use the named sketch/table in the directions. Label views, dimensions, units and revision.

40–85 min · Make · Numbered bench directions

  1. Cut, fold and tape each blank into a triangular tube with three 2-in faces. Keep both ends level.
  2. Stand the columns on the marked footprint, one under each side of the platform. Place the 6 × 6-in platform across them; tape its contacts lightly.
  3. Put the empty cup at the platform center. If it cannot support the cup, repair the column seams before recording a load trial.
  4. Add one paper clip every five seconds up to ten. Stop immediately if a column tips, folds or the platform falls; do not catch a falling load with the model.
  5. Unload. Cut two 6 × 1-in ties from offcuts. Tape one tie across the front column bases and one across the rear bases to resist spreading; do not tape the tower to the table.
  6. Repeat the same 0–10-clip test with the same cup, platform and placement. Record the cap if both versions hold ten.

Notebook: Label made parts and note any changed dimension. A short labeled sketch is enough; do not write an essay.

85–100 min · Test · Test and inspect

  1. Freestanding footprint no larger than 6 × 6 in; height 11 in ±1/4.
  2. Record last load held for five seconds and failure location. Ten clips means “held the test cap,” not “maximum strength is ten.”

Notebook: Copy the specified trial table; include each pass/fail or measured value and the change made.

100–110 min · Explain · Show the finished work

  1. Put these on the bench: One tower with two triangular columns and removable base ties.
  2. Two load records and an annotated load-path sketch.
  3. Complete the independent transfer problem below. These supplied numbers are practice values; they do not change the required build dimensions.

  5. Save one short individual answer with units, working and notebook page/date. Show the teacher your own physical measurement and plan interpretation. Store the labeled project and return shared supplies.

All crews use two equal blanks and identical loading increments. Check ties connect column bases, not the tabletop.

  1. Compare improvement against a baseline.
  2. Version 1 holds 4 identical objects; version 2 holds 7: (7 − 4)/4 × 100 = 75% more.
  3. Object count is a comparative load measure, not force in newtons. A capped test gives a lower bound on capacity.

60% increase. Footprint limit is 6 × 6 in. Strength depends on geometry, material, load path and stability; height alone is not evidence.

trades-etf-2.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

Make three equal-paper beams and compare midpoint deflection over the same 8-in gap.

Why: Cross-section changes stiffness without necessarily changing material quantity. You will measure that effect before choosing structural shapes.

  1. Three labeled beam shapes and one repeated sample.
  2. Notebook cross-sections and six test rows.

110 minutes / two periods. Seven crews for 15 students: six pairs and one trio. Rotate marker, maker and checker; each student keeps their own graph notebook and completes one digital transfer answer.

Daily kit and preparation

Per crew: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Three 10 × 3-in paper strips, two equal-height book stacks, one small paper cup with five large paper clips, and a vertical ruler.

Class quantities: prepare seven of these kits; each student has their own tape, pencil and notebook. Shared stations are identified explicitly above.

Project equipment and continuity

Show this before students start

  2. Make table: shape | unloaded height mm | loaded height mm | deflection mm | collapsed?

  1. Leave A flat. Fold B lengthwise at 1 1/2 in to make an open V. Fold C at 1 and 2 in to make a U-channel with a 1-in floor and upright sides.
  2. Place A with 1 in resting on each support. Mark its midpoint at 5 in from an end.
  3. Measure unloaded midpoint height. Place the same cup with five clips at the midpoint, release and measure after five seconds.
  4. Remove the load and repeat with B, ridge down so the cup bridges its upper edges, then C, channel opening up.
  5. Repeat the three tests once. If a beam collapses, record collapse instead of inventing a deflection.

  3. The clear gap excludes the supports; total member length includes both bearings.

  2. Measuring: observe the student place/read the tool using the specified datum and endpoints.

  2. I can survey a space and check model dimensions, openings and structural/thermal tests.
  3. I can interpret coordinated floor plans, elevations, details, symbols and scale.

  2. Measure twice, with roles swapped. Record both readings in feet/inches AND total inches. Keep the passage clear.

trades-etf-2.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

Build a separate 6 × 8-in joint-center frame, test its racking and add a diagonal brace; then reinforce the model room’s corners.

Why: A diagonal changes how a rectangular frame resists shape change. You will connect a measured test with a bracing decision.

  1. A braced test frame and four reinforced corners on the room model.
  2. Two diagonals and before/after racking data with a labeled frame sketch.

Class quantities: prepare seven of these kits; each student has their own tape, pencil and notebook. Shared stations are identified explicitly above.

Set up and rehearse the book fixture with the actual card. Use ten paper clips in the same cup for both tests, not an unspecified hand push. Stabilize book bases with another flat book if needed.

Project equipment and continuity

Use seven crew trays. Reserve a permitted classroom survey area. Collect the daily kits before release. Keep the supplied model dimensions separate from actual school measurements. These are classroom models, not full-size construction designs.

Show this before students start

Show the difference between a 9-in strip and its 8-in joint spacing. Hang the cup from the same top-right point twice; demonstrate how the ruler reads vertical movement.

Open labeled assembly / test drawing

  1. I can convert feet/inches, scale dimensions, and calculate building quantities and performance change.
  2. I can survey a space and check model dimensions, openings and structural/thermal tests.
  3. I can interpret coordinated floor plans, elevations, details, symbols and scale.
  4. I can build and improve a model building using structural and thermal test evidence.

0–10 min · Brief · Today’s exact job

  1. Why this job: A diagonal changes how a rectangular frame resists shape change. You will connect a measured test with a bracing decision.
  2. Required today: Build a separate 6 × 8-in joint-center frame, test its racking and add a diagonal brace; then reinforce the model room’s corners.

  1. Mark each strip centerline and points 1/2 in from its ends. Mark brace attachment centers 1/2 and 10 1/2 in from one end.
  2. Measure both frame diagonals between joint centers before the test; a square 6 × 8-in rectangle has two 10-in diagonals.

Notebook: Feature | required value | actual value | units | datum/endpoints. Keep repeat readings.

  1. Sketch the four joint centers as a 6 × 8-in rectangle. Draw the brace from bottom-left to top-right.
  2. Make table: unbraced / braced | starting top-right height | loaded height | downward movement, in mm.

  1. Arrange the two long strips horizontally and short strips vertically with center marks overlapping. Tape each overlap on both faces; keep joints flexible enough to rack.
  2. Stand the frame vertical. Sandwich its left upright between two upright books and tape it to the outer book face so both left joint centers stay fixed. Teacher checks the books are stable.

  4. Measure the top-right joint height from the tabletop before loading and after five seconds of load. Remove the cup.
  5. Return the frame to its original rectangular shape. Tape the diagonal between bottom-left and top-right centers; use the 11-in strip’s 1/2-in end allowances.
  6. Repeat with the identical cup/clip load and fixed left side.
  7. Fold each 2 × 2-in square into an angle bracket. Tape one inside each corner of the model room without blocking its door; label this model revision B.

  1. Compare vertical movement at the same joint under the same load. Report any movement too small to resolve with the ruler.
  2. Check the brace joins opposite joint centers and the room door still swings 90 degrees.

5 in by the Pythagorean relationship. The wall elevation shows the vertical-wall brace; the floor plan alone does not show its height.

trades-etf-2.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

Make a removable roof and a materials takeoff for the model’s walls, door opening and roof.

Why: Estimators subtract openings and distinguish surface area from purchased sheet quantities. A removable roof lets the next worker inspect the interior.

110 minutes / two periods. Seven crews for 15 students: six pairs and one trio. Rotate marker, maker and checker; each student keeps their own graph notebook and completes one digital transfer answer.

Daily kit and preparation

Per crew: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Model room, one 8 × 6-in card roof, two 2 × 1-in card locator strips and 12 in tape.

Class quantities: prepare seven of these kits; each student has their own tape, pencil and notebook. Shared stations are identified explicitly above.

Show this before students start

Demonstrate net area by shading the door opening. Show a roof tab under the lid instead of taping the roof permanently shut.

Learning targets

  1. I can convert feet/inches, scale dimensions, and calculate building quantities and performance change.
  2. I can survey a space and check model dimensions, openings and structural/thermal tests.
  3. I can interpret coordinated floor plans, elevations, details, symbols and scale.

  2. Draw the roof underside with two locator tabs near the north/south edges. These keep the roof from sliding; it stays lift-off.

  6. Write a small material label under the roof: nominal wall covering, roof area and actual card used.

trades-etf-2.title: P2 · 07 · Build and Test an Insulated Cup Enclosure
trades-etf-2.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

Make a two-layer paper enclosure for one ice cup and compare it with an identical uninsulated control cup.

Why: Envelope performance requires a fair comparison. You will keep starting ice, time and handling the same while changing the insulation.

  1. One insulated cup enclosure and one 4 × 4-in wall-layer sample.
  2. Actual control/test melt results, a section sketch and a supported comparison.

110 minutes / two periods. Seven crews for 15 students: six pairs and one trio. Rotate marker, maker and checker; each student keeps their own graph notebook and completes one digital transfer answer.

Daily kit and preparation

Per crew: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Two identical dry 240–250-mL plastic cups, two identical paper/card lids, two letter-paper sheets, tape, tray, timer, sieve, catch cup, 1-g balance and 120 g ice per crew (60 g for each cup). Shared balance station is acceptable.

Class quantities: prepare seven of these kits; each student has their own tape, pencil and notebook. Shared stations are identified explicitly above.

Collect matching cups, ice, a sieve and 1-g balance before release. Run one 20-minute preparation check to ensure melt is measurable in the room. If not, schedule a longer whole-class interval and print that single interval before class; do not improvise different times per crew.

Project equipment and continuity

Use seven crew trays. Reserve a permitted classroom survey area. Collect the daily kits before release. Keep the supplied model dimensions separate from actual school measurements. These are classroom models, not full-size construction designs.

Show this before students start

Demonstrate tare, equal starting mass and the 30-second drain. Explain that we weigh melt, not water plus cup, and that both cups receive identical lids.

Open labeled assembly / test drawing

Learning targets

  1. I can convert feet/inches, scale dimensions, and calculate building quantities and performance change.
  2. I can survey a space and check model dimensions, openings and structural/thermal tests.
  3. I can interpret coordinated floor plans, elevations, details, symbols and scale.
  4. I can build and improve a model building using structural and thermal test evidence.

0–10 min · Brief · Today’s exact job

  1. Why this job: Envelope performance requires a fair comparison. You will keep starting ice, time and handling the same while changing the insulation.
  2. Required today: Make a two-layer paper enclosure for one ice cup and compare it with an identical uninsulated control cup.
  3. Look at the supplied labeled drawing. Find the finished object or test setup before starting.
  4. Read the kit list. Take the listed continuing project out of storage; name missing items before beginning.

Notebook: Title/date; one sentence naming today’s exact object and its purpose.

10–25 min · Measure · Measure and mark

  1. Measure cup circumference with a paper strip, marking one full wrap; measure cup height with ruler.
  2. At the balance station tare each dry cup and add 60 g ice to each. Start both cups together.

Notebook: Feature | required value | actual value | units | datum/endpoints. Keep repeat readings.

25–40 min · Plan · Read the plan and work the math

  1. Draw a section: cup, two paper wrap layers and 1/2-in crumpled-paper bottom pad. Label the control’s matching lid.
  2. Prepare table: cup | starting ice g | elapsed min | collected melt g | observations. Test interval is 20 min.

Notebook: Use the named sketch/table in the directions. Label views, dimensions, units and revision.

40–85 min · Make · Numbered bench directions

  1. Cut two paper strips each cup-height tall and circumference + 1 in long. Tape them end-to-end if needed to reach that measured length.
  2. Wrap the test cup twice, one strip at a time, loosely enough to leave small air spaces; tape only the seams. Keep paper dry and outside the cup.
  3. Make a 1/2-in-thick lightly crumpled pad from remaining paper and place it under the test cup. Control sits directly on the same tray.
  4. Add the equal ice masses, put matching lids on both and start a 20-minute timer. Keep them side-by-side away from sun/vents.
  5. During the wait, make a 4 × 4-in two-layer wall sample for the model room and draw its layers; do not disturb cups.
  6. At 20 minutes drain each cup through the same sieve into the tared catch cup for 30 seconds. Weigh the collected melt, drying/taring the catch cup between samples.
  7. Calculate control melt minus insulated melt. Calculate percent reduction only if control melt is greater than zero; keep all readings even if insulation did worse.

Notebook: Label made parts and note any changed dimension. A short labeled sketch is enough; do not write an essay.

85–100 min · Test · Test and inspect

  1. Both start with 60 g ice, have the same lid and run for the same 20 minutes; record any deviation.
  2. Readings at/below the 1-g instrument resolution are inconclusive. Do not replace them with the worked example or claim an R-value.

Notebook: Copy the specified trial table; include each pass/fail or measured value and the change made.

100–110 min · Explain · Show the finished work

  1. Put these on the bench: One insulated cup enclosure and one 4 × 4-in wall-layer sample.
  2. Actual control/test melt results, a section sketch and a supported comparison.
  3. Complete the independent transfer problem below. These supplied numbers are practice values; they do not change the required build dimensions.
  4. A control melts 15 g and an insulated version melts 9 g in comparable trials. Find percent melt reduction. State one condition that must be held the same.
  5. Save one short individual answer with units, working and notebook page/date. Show the teacher your own physical measurement and plan interpretation. Store the labeled project and return shared supplies.

What exactly are we making or doing?

Operate air and water syringe pairs; attach a paper indicator and measure actual input/output travel.

Prepare seven compatible pairs. Use a spare water-filled syringe to flush each tube before joining under the tray waterline. Never fit needles. Confirm each plunger has at least 20 mm safe motion from its start.

Project equipment and continuity

Use seven matched syringe pairs and seven 60-cm tubes. Verify leak-free tube fit, easy hand travel and at least 20 mm usable stroke. Prepare the water pairs at input 15 mL/output 5 mL with a water-filled tube. Connect below the tray waterline to exclude air; wipe dry and check operation. No needles or heat. This course uses the syringe device throughout; a boat is not an alternative students must choose.

  4. Read the kit list. Take the listed continuing project out of storage; name missing items before beginning.

  1. Mark base datum A at lower-left; draw centerline y=3 in. Mark nozzle location x=3 in.
  2. With output at 5 mL, check there is room to its right for the 2-in sled deck plus at least 20 mm travel before the base edge. Teacher checks fit before taping.

  1. Label base, fixed barrel, two saddle straps, moving plunger, sled tab/deck and tube on the assembly sketch.
  2. Record two saddle locations on the smooth barrel, clear of nozzle, printed start reading and moving plunger/flange. These locations depend on the actual syringe body; measure and record them.

Notebook: Use the named sketch/table in the directions. Label views, dimensions, units and revision.

40–85 min · Make · Numbered bench directions

  1. Cut base to 12 × 6 in. Cut two 4 × 1-in saddle strips and sled blank 3 × 2 in.
  2. Fold sled across its 2-in width at 1 in from a short end. Stand the 1-in tab upright; the remaining 2 × 2-in deck lies on the base.
  3. Lay output on centerline, nozzle at x=3 in and pointing left. Keep its 5-mL start position.
  4. Curve each saddle over the fixed barrel, then crease its two ends down onto the base. Tape those ends firmly to the base. Do not tape or pinch the moving plunger.
  5. Put the sled tab against the right-facing flat thumb pad, deck extending right. Tape tab to pad on both accessible sides; the deck must slide flat rather than hang above the base.
  6. Route the 60-cm tube in a broad loop to input off the left side. Tape the tube loosely to the base near the nozzle for strain relief; never flatten the tube.
  7. Move input slowly 20 mm. Sled should travel right. Pull input back to return the sled; do not reset it by hand.
  8. Draw START at the sled’s front/right edge in the reset position and a delivery line 20 mm to its right. Put the paper cargo square on the deck.

Notebook: Label made parts and note any changed dimension. A short labeled sketch is enough; do not write an essay.

  1. Do three out-and-back cycles. The input hand is the only drive; output barrel stays fixed and sled clears the base edge.
  2. Record actual sled travel each time. Classroom acceptance for equal-syringe travel is 20 mm ±2 mm, after any bubble/mount repair; failures remain recorded.

Notebook: Copy the specified trial table; include each pass/fail or measured value and the change made.

  1. Put these on the bench: One water-powered sliding delivery sled with start/delivery marks and paper cargo.
  2. Dimensioned assembly sketch and three travel readings.
  3. Complete the independent transfer problem below. These supplied numbers are practice values; they do not change the required build dimensions.
  4. Input area 2 cm² moves 3 cm; output area is 3 cm². Predict output travel. Point to the mounting feature that prevents sideways motion.
  5. Save one short individual answer with units, working and notebook page/date. Show the teacher your own physical measurement and plan interpretation. Store the labeled project and return shared supplies.

Inspect each mount before water operation. Both students must locate a base coordinate and measure a stroke.

Sled tilts → refold tab 90 degrees and lower attachment so deck rests on base. Barrel creeps → tighten saddle end tape. Output jams → free plunger from saddle/tape; never force it. Bubbles → teacher reprimes.

  1. Predict travel with a larger output piston.
  2. A_in = 1 cm²; A_out = 2 cm²; input 4 cm: output = (1 × 4)/2 = 2 cm.
  3. Ideal output force would double, but do not claim you measured a force ratio without force measurements.

Output = (2 × 3)/3 = 2 cm. An actual guide/brace must be identified; ideal force claims require the model’s limitations.

trades-etf-3.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

At the prepared gravity station, time 15 mL of water through straight and curved routes; then secure a smooth tube route on the sled.

Why: Pipe work requires quantities and rates as well as a route drawing. A fair comparison controls starting head, tube and outlet height.

  1. A secured tube route on the sled and two measured route drawings.
  2. Six actual rates with conditions and a comparison limit.

Daily kit and preparation

Class quantities: prepare seven of these kits; each student has their own tape, pencil and notebook. Shared stations are identified explicitly above.

Build and rehearse the gravity station before class. If the 15-mL interval is shorter than reliable stopwatch timing, use slow-motion video timestamps at that station and teach that single timing method. Do not substitute made-up times. Run station groups while other crews inspect sled mounts.

Project equipment and continuity

Use seven matched syringe pairs and seven 60-cm tubes. Verify leak-free tube fit, easy hand travel and at least 20 mm usable stroke. Prepare the water pairs at input 15 mL/output 5 mL with a water-filled tube. Connect below the tray waterline to exclude air; wipe dry and check operation. No needles or heat. This course uses the syringe device throughout; a boat is not an alternative students must choose.

Show this before students start

Show the start/stop meniscus crossings and fixed vertical drop. Explain why 15 mL is used even though the barrel says 20 at the start.

Open labeled assembly / test drawing

  1. I can calculate displacement ratios, volume or distance rates, and performance change.
  2. I can measure device geometry and repeatable motion or flow with stated conditions.
  3. I can interpret fluid routes, assembly drawings, centerlines and parts lists.
  4. I can build, test, diagnose and physically improve a working fluid device.

0–10 min · Brief · Today’s exact job

  1. Why this job: Pipe work requires quantities and rates as well as a route drawing. A fair comparison controls starting head, tube and outlet height.
  2. Required today: At the prepared gravity station, time 15 mL of water through straight and curved routes; then secure a smooth tube route on the sled.
  3. Look at the supplied labeled drawing. Find the finished object or test setup before starting.
  4. Read the kit list. Take the listed continuing project out of storage; name missing items before beginning.

Notebook: Title/date; one sentence naming today’s exact object and its purpose.

10–25 min · Measure · Measure and mark

  1. Measure the reservoir 5-mL-line-to-outlet vertical drop as 10 cm and secure outlet at that height.
  2. Measure the same tube’s actual length 60 cm. Record bore only if the kit states it; do not guess from outside diameter.

Notebook: Feature | required value | actual value | units | datum/endpoints. Keep repeat readings.

25–40 min · Plan · Read the plan and work the math

  1. Sketch route A as one broad U and B as a broad S, with identical inlet/outlet locations and no uphill crest trapping air.
  2. Make table: route | trial | volume 15 mL | time s | rate mL/s. Three trials for each route.

Notebook: Use the named sketch/table in the directions. Label views, dimensions, units and revision.

40–85 min · Make · Numbered bench directions

  1. Teacher clamps the upright barrel and secures tube outlet over a cup in the tray.
  2. Fill tube completely with water first. Pinch the tube gently near its outlet while filling reservoir above the 20-mL mark.
  3. Release. Start the timer as the level crosses 20 mL; stop at 5 mL. Do not touch the reservoir during flow.
  4. Refill and repeat twice. Rotate reader/timer/recorder; pairs share the recording role.
  5. Rearrange only the middle of the tube into route B, maintaining length and both endpoint heights. Repeat three trials.
  6. Calculate 15 ÷ time for each valid trial. A tied result is acceptable; hand timing limits small comparisons.
  7. Reconnect the teacher-checked water pair on the sled. Route its tube in a broad untwisted loop and tape a loose guide to keep it away from the moving sled.

Notebook: Label made parts and note any changed dimension. A short labeled sketch is enough; do not write an essay.

85–100 min · Test · Test and inspect

  1. Three valid timed trials per route; same marks, tube and outlet height. Mark spills or bubbles invalid and repeat.
  2. The sled still performs three strokes after reconnection. Gravity-flow results do not directly predict syringe-machine speed under hand pressure.

Notebook: Copy the specified trial table; include each pass/fail or measured value and the change made.

  1. Put these on the bench: A secured tube route on the sled and two measured route drawings.
  2. Six actual rates with conditions and a comparison limit.
  3. Complete the independent transfer problem below. These supplied numbers are practice values; they do not change the required build dimensions.
  4. A system collects 200 mL in 25 s. Find average flow rate and identify two conditions to hold constant when comparing a second tube.
  5. Save one short individual answer with units, working and notebook page/date. Show the teacher your own physical measurement and plan interpretation. Store the labeled project and return shared supplies.

Notebook: Individual transfer calculation with units + page/date containing the practical evidence.

Check rates include mL/s and each crew has real station data. Do not claim U versus S must differ.

If the build does not work

Flow stops → check air bubble, pinched tube or outlet too high. Level passes before timer ready → refill and repeat. Changed tube length → invalidate comparison and restore 60 cm.

  1. Calculate an average collection rate.
  2. 180 mL in 15 s = 12 mL/s. At that average rate, 240 mL would take 20 s.
  3. A falling reservoir changes pressure head; the reported value is the trial’s average.

Teacher answer key and interpretation

8 mL/s. Constant starting head, liquid, tube bore when not the changed variable, collection method and timing are valid choices.

  1. Math: inspect the individual operation, units and reasonableness check.
  2. Measuring: observe the student place/read the tool using the specified datum and endpoints.
  3. Plan reading: ask the student to find one labeled dimension or connection on both drawing and object.

  2. I can measure device geometry and repeatable motion or flow with stated conditions.

  2. Add a parts list with two syringes, one 60-cm tube, base, two saddles, one sled and three fence strips.

  6. Exchange drawings; partner identifies all parts on the actual assembly using the labels.

  1. Cargo stays on deck for three complete cycles. Fence does not bind or reduce travel.
  2. Every listed part can be found on the drawing and object; moving and fixed parts are distinct.

Notebook: Copy the specified trial table; include each pass/fail or measured value and the change made.

100–110 min · Explain · Show the finished work

  1. Put these on the bench: A fenced delivery sled with a complete assembly drawing and parts list.
  2. Notebook includes centerline/offset measurements and three cargo trials.
  3. Complete the independent transfer problem below. These supplied numbers are practice values; they do not change the required build dimensions.

  3. Their centers lie 1 in and 2 in from the same edge.

trades-etf-3.title: P3 · 05 · Find and Repair a Loose Actuator Mount
trades-etf-3.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

Diagnose a deliberately loose saddle, repair it, and prove the sled repeats three accurate deliveries.

Why: Repair begins with an observed fault, a predicted cause and a controlled retest. Replacing random parts can hide the original problem.

  1. A repaired, stable sled with accessible connections.
  2. Notebook contains symptom, evidence, a named repair and retest readings.

110 minutes / two periods. Seven crews for 15 students: six pairs and one trio. Rotate marker, maker and checker; each student keeps their own graph notebook and completes one digital transfer answer.

Daily kit and preparation

Per crew: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Working sled, cargo square, ruler, towel and 12 in replacement tape. Teacher prepares one loose saddle end with power supplied only by hand input at rest.

Class quantities: prepare seven of these kits; each student has their own tape, pencil and notebook. Shared stations are identified explicitly above.

Use only the specified loose-saddle fault. Do not make leaks or pressure blockages as surprise faults. Return input/output to their marked reset positions.

Project equipment and continuity

Use seven matched syringe pairs and seven 60-cm tubes. Verify leak-free tube fit, easy hand travel and at least 20 mm usable stroke. Prepare the water pairs at input 15 mL/output 5 mL with a water-filled tube. Connect below the tray waterline to exclude air; wipe dry and check operation. No needles or heat. This course uses the syringe device throughout; a boat is not an alternative students must choose.

Show this before students start

Show that input motion may move an unsecured whole syringe instead of delivering useful plunger motion. Model observing first, repairing second.

Open labeled assembly / test drawing

Learning targets

  1. I can calculate displacement ratios, volume or distance rates, and performance change.
  2. I can measure device geometry and repeatable motion or flow with stated conditions.
  3. I can interpret fluid routes, assembly drawings, centerlines and parts lists.
  4. I can build, test, diagnose and physically improve a working fluid device.

0–10 min · Brief · Today’s exact job

  1. Why this job: Repair begins with an observed fault, a predicted cause and a controlled retest. Replacing random parts can hide the original problem.

  1. Draw a pencil witness line at the output barrel’s original position on the base.
  2. Measure barrel shift and sled travel during one gentle 20-mm input stroke. Stop if the mount releases.

Notebook: Feature | required value | actual value | units | datum/endpoints. Keep repeat readings.

25–40 min · Plan · Read the plan and work the math

  1. Make a fault table: symptom | suspected part | evidence | repair | retest.
  2. Circle the suspect saddle on the assembly drawing before touching its tape.

Notebook: Use the named sketch/table in the directions. Label views, dimensions, units and revision.

  1. Teacher peels one end of the rear saddle from the base; do not disconnect or obstruct the tube.
  2. Operate one gentle stroke while partner watches the barrel witness line. Record the symptom.
  3. Return input to its start; keep hands off the moving sled. Explain the suspected mount to your partner.
  4. Remove loose tape. Reposition barrel on centerline and nozzle datum, then retape the saddle end firmly.
  5. Dry the tray and outside connections with a towel. Inspect for fresh drops during three slow cycles; do not treat old tray water as new leakage.
  6. Run three cargo deliveries from the same start mark and measure actual travel each time.
  7. Add the repair and three results to the fault table.

85–100 min · Test · Test and inspect

  1. Barrel stays on its witness line and each travel is 20 mm ±2 mm. Record any remaining failure.
  2. A repair is complete only after the same motion test repeats without hands holding the output.

Notebook: Copy the specified trial table; include each pass/fail or measured value and the change made.

  2. Notebook contains symptom, evidence, a named repair and retest readings.
  3. Complete the independent transfer problem below. These supplied numbers are practice values; they do not change the required build dimensions.

  2. Start 200 mL; receiver 175 mL; liquid retained 20 mL: unaccounted volume = 5 mL.
  3. Do not call all 25 mL missing from the receiver a leak.

5 mL. Check retained liquid, spills, measurement resolution and starting/ending conditions.

trades-etf-3.title: P3 · 06 · Time Five Delivery Cycles
trades-etf-3.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

Record three timed trials of five complete cargo-delivery cycles on the unchanged sled.

Why: A baseline needs a repeatable definition. We will time the same task before and after a later mechanical change.

  1. Unchanged working sled revision A and a baseline timing record.
  2. Three rates, mean time and exact cycle definition.

110 minutes / two periods. Seven crews for 15 students: six pairs and one trio. Rotate marker, maker and checker; each student keeps their own graph notebook and completes one digital transfer answer.

Daily kit and preparation

Per crew: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Sled revision A, same paper cargo, stopwatch, ruler and trial sheet.

Class quantities: prepare seven of these kits; each student has their own tape, pencil and notebook. Shared stations are identified explicitly above.

Rehearse endpoint visibility. A short strip of contrasting tape makes the sled edge easier to see; do not change travel to make timing easier.

Project equipment and continuity

Use seven matched syringe pairs and seven 60-cm tubes. Verify leak-free tube fit, easy hand travel and at least 20 mm usable stroke. Prepare the water pairs at input 15 mL/output 5 mL with a water-filled tube. Connect below the tray waterline to exclude air; wipe dry and check operation. No needles or heat. This course uses the syringe device throughout; a boat is not an alternative students must choose.

Show this before students start

Demonstrate one complete cycle and one incomplete cycle. Say why an outstroke alone is not a complete out-and-back cycle.

Open labeled assembly / test drawing

Learning targets

  1. I can calculate displacement ratios, volume or distance rates, and performance change.
  2. I can measure device geometry and repeatable motion or flow with stated conditions.
  3. I can interpret fluid routes, assembly drawings, centerlines and parts lists.
  4. I can build, test, diagnose and physically improve a working fluid device.

0–10 min · Brief · Today’s exact job

  1. Why this job: A baseline needs a repeatable definition. We will time the same task before and after a later mechanical change.
  2. Required today: Record three timed trials of five complete cargo-delivery cycles on the unchanged sled.
  3. Look at the supplied labeled drawing. Find the finished object or test setup before starting.
  4. Read the kit list. Take the listed continuing project out of storage; name missing items before beginning.

Notebook: Title/date; one sentence naming today’s exact object and its purpose.

10–25 min · Measure · Measure and mark

  1. Verify START-to-DELIVERY separation is 20 mm; use the same sled edge at both marks.
  2. Reset input/output and check barrel witness line before each timed trial.

Notebook: Feature | required value | actual value | units | datum/endpoints. Keep repeat readings.

25–40 min · Plan · Read the plan and work the math

  1. Make table: trial | five cycles complete? | total time s | cycles/s | faults.
  2. Practice one untimed trial. The aim is consistent complete travel, not forceful racing.

Notebook: Use the named sketch/table in the directions. Label views, dimensions, units and revision.

40–85 min · Make · Numbered bench directions

  1. Put cargo on deck. Operator holds input; timer watches the sled edge and calls “ready.”
  2. Timer says “go” and starts clock as operator begins. Count a cycle only when sled reaches DELIVERY and returns to START.
  3. Stop timer at the fifth return. If a cycle misses either mark, label trial invalid and record the missed endpoint.
  4. Reset and repeat until there are three valid trials; retain invalid trials with reasons.
  5. Rotate roles so each student operates and measures. Use gentle motion and the same cargo throughout.
  6. Calculate 5 ÷ elapsed seconds for each trial. Calculate mean total time from the three valid trials.
  7. Inspect the sled without modifying it. Mark the two side-fence top edges as tomorrow’s guide-rail reference.

Notebook: Label made parts and note any changed dimension. A short labeled sketch is enough; do not write an essay.

85–100 min · Test · Test and inspect

  1. Three valid five-cycle trials; every endpoint reached. No direct pushing of output.
  2. All rates use cycles/s, not cm/s. Record observed spread rather than reporting a single fastest run.

Notebook: Copy the specified trial table; include each pass/fail or measured value and the change made.

100–110 min · Explain · Show the finished work

  1. Put these on the bench: Unchanged working sled revision A and a baseline timing record.
  2. Three rates, mean time and exact cycle definition.

Add two fixed low guide rails beside the sled’s path, then repeat the same five-cycle timing test.

Locate a 5-mm mounting error, restore the supplied assembly and repeat measured travel.

Use seven matched syringe pairs and seven 60-cm tubes. Verify leak-free tube fit, easy hand travel and at least 20 mm usable stroke.   2. Schematic, route lengths and five OFF/ON test rows.

Daily kit and preparation

Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. 3-V two-AA switched holder, one 3-V lamp/holder, three alligator leads, one wooden spring clothespin, two 1 × 2-in foil strips, base 10 × 8 in, fixed wall 4 × 4 in, door 3 × 4 in, 1 × 3-in thin-card tongue and 24 in tape.

Obtain seven complete kits and test one two-lamp parallel circuit with the chosen holder before release. Use 3-V-rated miniature filament lamps; bare LEDs are not substitutes for this recipe. Maximum classroom supply is two AA cells in the specified holder. Label lamp terminals A/B, switches 1/2, and supply +/−. Prepare one supervised meter station and label its actual sockets/range; use the instrument manual. Do not release meter lessons without that station.

  1. On the 10 × 8 base use the front-left corner as (0,0). Mark wall line y=3 in and hinge point (4,3). Mark tongue strip 1 × 3 in and fold 1 in from a short end.
  2. Measure actual lead routes with a string along bends; record each run and 2-in classroom connection allowance separately from available lead length.

  1. Copy J1’s three connections with terminal labels. Trace the entire loop before attaching battery leads.
  2. Sketch door shut/tongue inserted (lamp off) and door open/tongue out (lamp on).

  2. Tape the 3 × 4-in door to the wall’s right vertical edge. Shut, it runs from x=4 to x=7 along y=3. It opens toward the FRONT of the base (smaller y).

trades-etf-4.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

Improve the same detector with a tongue guide and verify ten repeatable door-open signals.

Why: Reliability is repeatable operation under a stated procedure. You will fix alignment and distinguish circuit connectivity from physical placement.

trades-etf-4.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

At the supervised station, insert the meter into one break in the lamp circuit, record current, then restore the detector.

Why: Current measurement requires the circuit’s charge flow to pass through the instrument. This is a different connection from voltage measurement.

  2. Work the supplied resistor example as a MODEL exercise; the filament lamp is not a constant 30-ohm resistor.

  1. Switch holder OFF and remove the original switch-to-lamp lead.
  2. Teacher connects switch output to the meter current input and meter COM to lamp A, using the actual instrument’s fused rated input.
  3. Teacher inspects the complete loop and selected current range, then permits holder ON with tongue out.
  4. Each student reads and records current. Turn holder OFF before touching any wiring.
  5. Teacher removes meter and restores the original switch-to-lamp lead. Return red meter lead to its V socket for storage.
  6. Run three detector OFF/ON cycles to confirm restoration.
  7. Compare the measured current with the stated lamp rating as an observation; do not force an Ohm-law match using an invented resistance.

  1. Every current reading includes unit and supervised series connection. No student experiments with meter sockets under power.
  2. Detector works after meter removal; original loop is fully restored.

trades-etf-4.bodyHtml:
What exactly are we making or doing?

Build a two-room card model on an 8 × 6-in base; wire each 3-V lamp through its own switch in parallel.

110 minutes / two periods. Seven crews for 15 students: six pairs and one trio. Rotate marker, maker and checker; each student keeps their own graph notebook and completes one digital transfer answer.

Daily kit and preparation

Per crew: Each student: tape measure, pencil and graph notebook. Per crew: ruler, scissors and masking tape. Prepared control exhibit, operator card, notebook and final drawings; teacher roster for four separate skill checks.

Class quantities: prepare seven of these kits; each student has their own tape, pencil and notebook. Shared stations are identified explicitly above.

Use a 15-student roster with four columns. Schedule brief individual checks throughout Make/Test, about 3 minutes each while other crews exhibit or retry. Keep the physical measurement prompt fresh for each student.

Project equipment and continuity

Obtain seven complete kits and test one two-lamp parallel circuit with the chosen holder before release. Use 3-V-rated miniature filament lamps; bare LEDs are not substitutes for this recipe. Maximum classroom supply is two AA cells in the specified holder. Label lamp terminals A/B, switches 1/2, and supply +/−. Prepare one supervised meter station and label its actual sockets/range; use the instrument manual. Do not release meter lessons without that station.

Show the four things the individual check requires. Model naming a datum and units before reading the tape. Explain that a missing observation is a next check, not automatic crew credit.
